item.title: The Therapeutic Uses of Writing
item.description:
Therapy

The Therapeutic Uses of Writing

Writing can be a creative, cathartic, or strategic adjunct to growth.

Posted July 8, 2026

Key points
  • There are various types of writing that can provide therapeutic benefits.
  • Writing about traumatic memories has been found to promote more positive mental health.
  • Writing in the morning, by hand, can be a very clarifying and intentional way to start each day.
  • In cognitive behavior therapy, writing is essential to the process of data collection and tracking progress.

Recently, a colleague asked me to share the ways I have used writing in my therapeutic work with clients over the years.
It's an excellent question. I have been a therapist for a long time, but I now also spend most of my time writing, and I am keenly aware of the myriad ways writing has assisted me at every point in my journey.

His question brought back memories of when I gave clients prescriptions to write, and it produced salutary results. It also led me to seek the wisdom of some reliable voices on the topic. Here are a few applications of writing in healing.

Valuing and connecting to the inner life

The decision to begin writing down what has been carried unspoken inside the soul can be a life-altering experience in itself. It requires intentionally--and hopefully, unapologetically--creating time and space for oneself. Taking time to write in an uncensored, unhurried way makes a statement that the inner life is valuable and deserves examination. The soul should be heard, and one of the best ways to give it voice is through writing.

Healing trauma
In the literature, the use of writing in a systematic way to promote therapeutic growth and heal the effects of trauma dates to the 1980s. Specifically, to a test administered by a psychology professor, James Pennebaker, at the University of Texas. Pennebaker’s experiment was simple. He asked his students to identify a traumatic or painful event from childhood. Then, he divided the class into three groups, which wrote for 15 minutes per day for four consecutive days. The first group wrote about current events in their lives. The second group wrote only factual details about the traumatic memory. The third group wrote about their thoughts, feelings, and the perceived impact of the traumatic event in the years since it occurred.

article continues after advertisement

It won’t surprise you to learn that the third group reported remarkable improvements in their physical and emotional health in the months that followed, results not enjoyed by the members of the other two groups. They made discoveries about themselves and realized, in some cases, the cost to their health of having kept these memories repressed for so long.

Letter writing
One tool that I have used often in therapy is letter-writing. Bessel Van der Kolk, a foremost scholar and clinician in the area of healing complex trauma, expresses well what many have come to know through practice.

"Most of us have poured out our hearts in angry, accusatory, plaintive, or sad letters after people have betrayed or abandoned us. Doing so almost always makes us feel better, even if we never send them."

Van de Kolk asserts the importance of writing by hand. Most of us these days find typing on a keyboard much more efficient than writing by hand. But that is the point. It is not about speed or efficiency. Just as our tone of voice changes when we pass through different emotional states while speaking aloud, our handwriting might change dramatically in the process of writing our feelings. This gives further evidence of issues most in need of care and healing.

In my practice, I have observed the therapeutic effect of writing letters, not to be sent, but simply as an opportunity for clients to fully process all of the feelings they may have about themselves and the person on the other side of a relationship.

After writing between sessions, in some cases, clients read their letters aloud in session, compounding the healing experience by hearing themselves say the insights they have written. This provides a powerful opportunity to discover new layers of understanding, compassion, and even forgiveness.

Morning Pages
Author Julia Cameron is known for promoting the practice of writing what she calls Morning Pages. This practice consists of writing three pages of spontaneous, uncensored thoughts, first thing every morning, by hand, not to be read by anyone else. The writing can be about everything or anything. It is writing down a three-page stream of consciousness as the first task of the day.

article continues after advertisement

Morning pages writing is not exclusively a therapeutic practice, but Cameron cites its many healthful benefits, including uncluttering the mind, releasing creative energy, becoming more honest, and finding direction for the day and the future. It can open a connection to one's higher power. She writes, "I like to think of [Morning Pages] as windshield wipers, wiping away anything that stands between you and a clear view of your day—a whisk broom that dislodges dust from every corner of our lives. The pages notify both us and the universe precisely where we are. I often think of them as a form of active meditation.”

That sounds like a sound mental health practice for anyone.

Data Collection

When cognitive behavior therapy is the primary modality in therapy, writing of a different type is essential to progress. In the initial phase of therapy, I ask clients to imagine themselves as researchers, with themselves as the research subject. Between sessions, they are instructed to become highly attuned to the events, conversations, and challenges in their daily lives, especially those that elicit strong feelings. They write down the events, how they responded, what they felt, and what they did.

In session, we will process one or more of the events they've written about and begin to identify the automatic or underlying thoughts that trigger strong emotions in specific circumstances. In this way, we facilitate clients' ability to "think about what they think about."

Clients write out these thoughts in all permutations they can find across many domains in their lives. Therapy then can focus on adjusting unproductive, pain-producing thought patterns and replacing them with more positive and constructive ones, which are then observed and tested in real life, with outcomes written down.

This accumulation of written data provides a record of progress in self-discovery and behavior change. We see that whether writing is for the purpose of clarifying the mind, unleashing creativity, coming to honesty about oneself, healing trauma, or tracking thoughts and feelings, it is a valuable practice in maintaining positive mental and spiritual health.

Psychology Today contributor Dr. Frank Anderson sums this up beautifully.

"Writing is a powerful medium because we don’t write at the same pace as we think. It forces us to slow down and be with memories and experiences in a way that gives us a novel perspective, a unique angle, or an observer's view of a memory or moment in our lives. Writing accesses different parts of the brain compared with the spoken word, so it allows us to articulate and share something that we’ve gone through in a new way."

I heartily endorse the practice of writing every day as a way of staying connected to our inner selves, staying clear about who we are and what we desire our lives to be.

item.title: Know Your Triggers and Admit Your Abusive Behavior
item.description:
Emotional Abuse

Know Your Triggers and Admit Your Abusive Behavior

Two more steps toward changing abusive behavior.

Posted July 8, 2026

Key points
  • There are certain external factors that can remind you of past trauma and "trigger" abusive behavior.
  • Discovering your particular triggers will help explain why it is that you sometimes become abusive.
  • Admitting and naming your abusive behavior can be extremely healing for both your victim(s) and for yourself.

This is the fifth in a series on how to identify and eliminate abusive behavior.

Step 4: Determining what your triggers are

Abusive behavior often occurs after you have encountered a trigger in your current environment. A trigger is anything your mind perceives to be similar to a past traumatic event, such as a location, tone of voice, topic of conversation, or a scene in a movie. Many triggers are interpersonal; for example, perceived rejection, abandonment, criticism, boundary violations, and yelling or mistreatment are common interpersonal triggers. Other triggers may be non-personal, such as certain sounds, smells, and tastes.

Because it is common to become emotionally abusive (yelling at your partner, blaming your partner, becoming overly critical, or other behaviors) after you have been triggered, you can ascertain exactly what your triggers are.

Exercise: Spot Your Triggers

  • Begin by creating a triggers list, noting the situations, environments, and times that typically set you off.
  • I have provided a list of the most common triggers that those who have a history of neglect or abuse in childhood have. Read the list carefully and put a check mark next to each item that tends to trigger you.

Common Triggers for Those Who Have Become Abusive

  • Feeling abandoned or rejected
  • People in authority
  • Competition
  • Feeling like someone is lying to you
  • Someone acting like they are better than you
  • Someone who reminds you of your mother
  • Someone who reminds you of your father
  • Someone who reminds you of an abuser
  • Being let down by someone
  • Being laughed at
  • Being accused of something you did not do
  • Being ignored
  • Feeling alone
  • The sound of someone crying
  • Being criticized
  • Someone is very angry
  • Someone is saying mean or abusive things to you
  • Someone yelling at you
  • Someone raising their hand or fist near you
  • Someone threatening to hurt you
  • Mean or dirty looks
  • Seeing violence on television, at the movies, or on the internet

Knowing your particular triggers can help you better understand yourself and your reactions. In particular, it can help you understand why you may become emotionally abusive.

Step 5: Admit your abusive behavior to those you have hurt or harmed. While it can be difficult to admit to yourself that you have been abusive, admitting it to your partner or your children may seem impossible. This is especially true for those of you who have difficulty admitting when you are wrong. You may be accustomed to denying your poor behavior, putting up a defensive wall to protect yourself from the criticism of others. And it is especially difficult to recognize how you have hurt or damaged those you love. The shame you feel when you do these things can be overwhelming, and since you likely experienced a great deal of shame when you were growing up, it may seem almost impossible to complete this step. You may repeatedly push away the truth and go back into denial. One thing that may help is to remind yourself that being vulnerable and being honest about the mistakes you’ve made in life will actually help you to heal your shame.

Admitting to your partner that you have been abusive will serve several purposes: First, it will help you continue to come out of denial. Dealing with your abusiveness can be so painful and so shame-inducing that you may be constantly tempted to minimize the damage you’ve caused or talk yourself out of facing up to it. But by admitting it to your partner (or older child), you make it harder to deny it in the future.

You also owe it to your partner (or older child) to admit that you have been abusive. They have been suffering from the effects of your behavior for some time now, and they may or may not realize it is abusive. If they don’t understand that they have been abused, they deserve to know. They need to be able to put a name to what they have been enduring, and they need to be able to stop thinking they are crazy or that they have been imagining it all along. They need to know so they can get some help for the debilitating effects of the abuse. Even if they have known they were being abused, they need you to admit it to confirm their feelings and perceptions. And in many cases, they may need confirmation so they can stop blaming themselves for all the relationship problems and for your abusive behavior.

Finally, you need to admit that you’ve been abusive because you need to take responsibility for your actions. I suggest you do so as directly and in as straightforward a manner as possible. Don’t beat around the bush: don’t try to slip it into a conversation casually. Give this the respect and significance it deserves. Here are some suggestions for making this a meaningful endeavor:

  • Tell your partner or older child that you have something important to tell them, or make an appointment to talk when you both won’t be distracted. Face your partner or child and look them directly in the eye.
  • Make sure you include all the following:
    1) A clear statement acknowledging that you have been abusive.
    2) Specific examples of your abusive behavior.
    3) Acknowledgement about how your behavior has hurt or damaged the other person.
    4) A statement of regret and remorse for your abusive behavior or attitude.
    5) a promise to work on changing
  • Be careful that you don’t make excuses or blame the person you have harmed in any way for your own behavior. Take full responsibility for your actions. You may explain why it is that you feel you became abusive, but stress that it is you and you alone who are responsible for your behavior and for changing your behavior.

This can be the most important step you can take toward your own healing and the healing of your relationships. It is also the most loving, unselfish thing you can do for your partner or older child, and it will be tremendously beneficial for your own recovery.

Steps 6 and 7 will follow in a separate post.

item.title: "The Invite" and the Costs of Shaming Our True Selves
item.description:
Perfectionism

"The Invite" and the Costs of Shaming Our True Selves

Self-oriented perfectionism and the lack of empathy for oneself.

Posted July 8, 2026

Key points
  • Self-oriented perfectionists often struggle with feeling empathy and compassion for themselves.
  • "The Invite" shows us how our shame around our needs may harm ourselves and others.
  • Our choices may bring us closer to or further away from acknowledging and fulfilling our needs.

Extreme lack of empathy is one of the defining traits of narcissism and psychopathy. It means that an individual is unable to place themself in another’s shoes to imagine how their decisions affect them; they can only grasp how their choices affect themself. (Arguably, they understand it, but can’t feel the pain they cause.) Many of these people are other-oriented perfectionists, demanding and unconcerned with how their expectations and punishments are received. (For clarity: Not every other-oriented perfectionist is narcissistic or psychopathic.) Those whom we would call self-oriented perfectionists have the opposite problem. While many of them exhibit a significant amount of empathy for others, they often have little left over for themselves, many believing they don't deserve it. (Of course, you can be both a self-oriented and other-oriented perfectionist.)

Self-oriented perfectionism is defined, in part, by a lack of empathy, too; a lack of empathy for oneself. Furthermore, if you can’t feel your own pain (or at least take it seriously), you’re also unable to gift yourself compassion. The new film, The Invite, which highlights the struggles of two couples who find themselves interlocked in an existential dialogue for one evening (one of them even jokes about its existential nature), is a window into this sort of stunted empathy. While much of the conversation revolves around sex and its variations, there are poignant moments pointing to deeper fears and longings.

In the film’s most insightful scene, Hawk, played by Edward Norton, recounts his experience of losing his wife to cancer. He tells the other three that, during their marriage, while his wife was sexually curious and explorative, he was, in contrast, sexually rigid. Therefore, he says, he repeatedly rejected her requests to experiment. Then, one day, the room fell permanently silent, and he realized he had to learn to live with the pain of knowing she would never feel accepted by him. So, he maintains, he resolved to explore his sexuality, and found joy in a variety of new experiences. While it’s obvious that Hawk had little empathy for his partner, he also denied himself pleasures that he would someday enjoy.

As the film progresses, Pina, the psychotherapist in the group, observes that Joe and Angela argue so much because they blame each other for their problems while continuously making decisions that contribute to them. So, here we have other-oriented perfectionism, which projects one’s own guilt elsewhere, onto another, expecting and demanding they take full responsibility for something that isn’t completely their fault. But, beneath the lack of empathy for the other is a lack of empathy for oneself. Joe and Angela won’t allow themselves to accept what they’ve deprived themselves of while maintaining their marriage; awareness of their own needs may feel threatening. And becoming aware of having to express them may feel even scarier. It’s easier to just blame your partner for your unhappiness than feel ashamed of yourself for your choices and vulnerabilities, or those needs you can’t seem to extinguish.

We can surmise that Hawk chose his partner because she was more sexually liberated than he was, rather than infer that he just discovered this new, cool thing he really liked. Hawk chose her over and over again, knowing she had a side to her that, on the surface, repelled him. We can imagine Hawk fantasizing about her giving him permission to express that part of himself, and we can imagine some deeper part of him coming to the surface to express gratitude in return. Pushing her away with his moralistic rigidity and scorn was a mechanism for suppressing his more primal side. And while he expressed sadness over how that must have made her feel, one can express an equal amount of sympathy for him for having rejected himself.

And we can extend that sympathy to Joe and Angela, who’ve also rejected themselves, each choosing a partner who shows little interest in the other’s inner life. Fundamentally, our choices often indicate how we see ourselves. While Joe and Angela didn’t reflect one another in their marriage, Hawk’s previous wife reflected him. And, with Pina, who had a similar sexual appetite, Hawk was able to freely acknowledge his need. To be clear, I’m not saying that every aspect of self-imposed perfectionism is bad or unhealthy. But Hawk’s rigidity is often seen in self-oriented perfectionists, who struggle with black-and-white thinking.

To Hawk, the world had no grey area, at least in this realm. To him, sexuality wasn’t a spectrum from normal to unusual to deviant to downright immoral. Everything that wasn’t the norm was to be shunned, despite his own apparent longings. For perfectionists, staring at their shame is akin to staring into an abyss, symbolic of their potential lives, unmet needs, and inability to fully reshape either one. Challenging one’s perfectionistic tendencies is a difficult road because perfectionists often struggle to disentangle who they are from whom they’re expected to be. In the film, Hawk paves that road for us. Sometimes, when trying something that may feel repugnant, we may discover a hidden need. Sometimes, when taking responsibility for a choice, we may discover that it’s actually a bridge bringing us closer to that need. Also, however, a choice is made to keep us apart from it.

item.title: Reality Is Potentiality
item.description:
Philosophy

Reality Is Potentiality

How minds distill actuality from possibility (and treat it as real).

Posted July 8, 2026

Key points
  • Reality may be, not actuality (concrete objects and events), but potentiality (possibilities).
  • Minds weave coherent worldviews by crystallizing potentiality into narratives: tapestries of actuality.
  • Creative minds delve into this sea of potentiality to actualize new ideas.
  • Meaning-making occurs by forging a more coherent worldview (a more stable tapestry of actuality).

The idea that reality is fundamentally made of possibilities grew out of puzzles in modern physics that seem to point toward a radically different way of thinking about reality.

It’s now been a century since physics revealed deep flaws in our everyday conception of reality. If you measure one property of a particle first (such as its spin), and then another (say, its velocity), you can get a different outcome than if you measured these properties in the reverse order. The answer depends on the order in which you ask the questions. Moreover, in quantum mechanics, probabilities are used not because we lack information (such as when you calculate the probability that your opponent has the ace of spades), but because that information doesn’t yet exist! (These are actually two sides of the same coin; that is, if there is no fully specified underlying state before measurement, then both order effects and irreducible probabilities follow naturally.)

Interestingly, psychologists discovered something remarkably similar about the human mind. In a field known as quantum cognition, researchers found that people's decisions often depend on the order in which different considerations are brought to mind. Ask someone first about one aspect of a political candidate and then another, and you may obtain a different judgment than if the order is reversed. Classical theories of decision-making struggle to explain such order effects, whereas the mathematical framework developed for quantum theory often predicts them surprisingly well. This doesn’t mean the brain is a quantum computer. But it suggests that both physical systems and human judgments may evolve from states of potential rather than reveal pre-existing answers. In other words, potential states are more fundamental than actual ones.

One attempt to make sense of this is physicist David Deutsch's many-worlds interpretation of quantum mechanics. In this view, each possible outcome occurs, but in a different universe; i.e., every quantum event causes reality to branch. Somewhere, there’s another version of you who ate something else for breakfast, and another Earth where history unfolded along another path, and so forth. It’s a provocative solution, but there’s another possible solution that to my mind is more elegant. It’s arrived at, not by asking (as physicists do), "What do the equations actually describe?" but by asking (as a psychologist), "Why does the world appear to us as it does?"

Tendrils of Actuality in a Sea of Potentiality

In this view, instead of countless fully realized worlds—i.e., worlds of actuality consisting of objects that genuinely exist and events that really happen—there’s just one world, and its fundamental nature is not actuality but potentiality. Actual events continually crystallize out of this vast tapestry of potential like the delicate fractal ice crystals that spread across the edge of a half-frozen body of water.

The idea grew in part from early research carried out with my Ph.D. supervisor on context-driven actualization of potential (Gabora & Aerts, 2005): how entities change over time by actualizing states made possible by their context, situation, or environment. If all this sounds impossibly abstract, it may be because our minds evolved to hide from us the fact that what we perceive as reality isn't real. Nervous systems evolved not to reveal the universe as it is but to help organisms survive long enough to reproduce. Each species perceives the sliver of reality that matters for its way of life, and assumes these perceptions to be reality itself. Bees see ultraviolet patterns on flowers that are invisible to us. Bats navigate using echoes. Increasingly, psychologists view human perception as less like a camera and more like a user interface. It presents us not with reality as it is, but a simplified representation that fosters successful action.

Our everyday experience of actuality may be part of that interface.

Minds Dwell in Actuality (but Now and Then Dip Into Potentiality)

The process of freezing potentiality into actuality occurs not only in perception but in thought. The moment we describe something, whether through language, music, painting, or even mathematics, we turn it into a narrative. We decide where the story begins, what details matter, how events connect, and what they mean. Even the most faithful account of an experience is still an interpretation. Our minds weave such narratives into what psychologists call a worldview—an integrated internal model of the world and our place within it. Each new experience is evaluated with respect to this ever-changing web of meanings. As we encounter new ideas and possibilities, we’re subconsciously wondering not so much, "Is this true?" but "Does this fit?" As I see it, coherence is our practical criterion for reality (Vieira & Gabora, 2026).

In this way, our worldviews generate streams of conscious experience by solidifying strands of actuality—objects, events, memories, explanations—from a sea of unrealized possibilities. These frozen trajectories of actuality successfully guide our actions and steer us into the future, but because they’re how we inhabit reality, we mistake them for reality itself.

Implications for Creativity

Seen this way, creativity acquires a new significance. Creativity consists of shepherding potentialities into actualities. Most of us spend our lives traveling well-established paths through actuality, but creative people linger longer in the surrounding realm of possibility. They tolerate ambiguity, entertain unlikely connections, and postpone certainty until patterns in their minds have had sufficient time to develop and mature. Society needs both; it needs people firmly anchored in actuality because coordinated action depends on shared understandings of what is real. But it also needs people who periodically drift into possibility, because tomorrow's ideas do not yet exist as actualities. Every scientific theory or work of art, every technological invention or ritualistic behavior, begins as a possibility before becoming part of the actuality we collectively inhabit (Carbert et al., 2014; Gabora & Saab, 2011; Scotney et al, 2020).

Implications for Meaning-making

Thinking of reality as potentiality can also impact the meaning-making process by which we understand and make sense of our lives. We often experience the past as though it were a chain of hardened events leading inevitably to the present. Every mistake seems permanent. Every missed opportunity feels like a door forever closed. Every loss appears absolute. But perhaps this sense of inevitability is itself part of the user interface our minds construct. The actual path we travelled is only one crystallization through a rich landscape of possibilities. By traveling it, we may alter the shape of the realm of potentiality, pulling some possibilities closer, into the adjacent possible: the possibilities that are made newly reachable because of what has already become actual. Unrealized possibilities don’t really disappear; they can shape how we interpret the past, imagine the future, and find meaning. Even grief changes under this perspective. Death remains real, and loss remains painful, but a life need not be understood merely as a fixed sequence of completed events. It also consists of possibilities awakened in others, possibilities left unfinished, and possibilities still unfolding through the lives it touched.

All this may be wrong; reality may ultimately be nothing more than the relentless unfolding of actual events. But I suspect that actuality is what our survival-oriented minds extract from an inexhaustible sea of potentiality. In this view, our worldviews aren't mirrors of reality, but living webs of meaning that crystallize coherent strands of actuality from that sea of potential. If so, reality itself is not those strands of actuality but the potentiality from which they continually emerge.

item.title: What the DSM Can't See
item.description:
DSM

What the DSM Can't See

Psychiatry's bible was built to describe suffering, not to explain it.

Posted July 8, 2026

Key points
  • The DSM revolution of 1980 gave psychiatry a common language by abandoning the search for underlying causes.
  • Even the architects of psychiatry's diagnostic system have acknowledged its fundamental limits.
  • The DSM achieved diagnostic agreement among clinicians but not proof that its categories match real diseases.
  • Between description and disease there is a gap. Patients live in that gap.
Source: Jakub Zerdzicki/Pexels

In the summer of 2016, I sat across from a clinician who asked me a series of questions. Had I been sleeping poorly? Had I lost interest in activities I once enjoyed? Did I feel worthless or guilty? Had I experienced changes in appetite, concentration, or energy?

I answered yes to enough of the questions to receive a diagnosis: major depressive disorder.

What no one asked—what the instrument in front of them was not designed to ask—was whether the depression I was describing was the whole story, or one face of something larger and more dangerous that the checklist could not see. It could not see the bipolar disorder beneath the depressive episode. It could not see the syphilis infection rewriting my neurology from the inside. It saw what it was built to see: symptoms, arranged in clusters, matched to a label.

The checklist those clinicians were using came from a book. That book—the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, or DSM is the subject of today's post. Last week, I described what it felt like to wear a diagnosis that didn't fit. This week, I want to look at the manual that cut the coat.

The Man Who Built Psychiatry's Bible

Allan Frances was once called "perhaps the most powerful psychiatrist in America" by The New York Times. He chaired the task force that built the DSM-IV (1994)—the book that determined which forms of suffering counted as mental illness, which treatments insurers would cover, and which diagnoses would follow millions of patients through the rest of their lives.

Years later, the psychologist Gary Greenberg asked Frances a simple question: could he define what a mental disorder actually was?

Frances's answer has followed him ever since. "There's no definition of a mental disorder," he said. "And it's bullshit. I mean, you can't define it."

He later clarified that he meant the bright line is impossible to draw—that good clinicians must exercise judgment where science cannot yet provide certainty. But the admission stood. The bible of the field had been built on a foundation its own architects could not fully describe.

How We Got Here

The DSM-III, which appeared in 1980, was designed to save psychiatry from itself. Its architect, Robert Spitzer, had watched the field spend decades under the influence of psychoanalysis—a framework that could explain almost anything and predict almost nothing. "Psychiatry was regarded as bogus," Spitzer said. He believed the field would only survive if it was "accepted as a medical discipline."

His solution was radical. The DSM-III excised the language of Freud entirely—no more neuroses, no more unconscious motivations, no more speculation about underlying causes. In its place, Spitzer installed something that looked like science: a taxonomy of discrete disorders, each defined by a checklist of observable symptoms. If a patient met, for example, five of seven criteria, she received a diagnosis.

The result, as Greenberg described it, was a transformation. The spiral-bound, 134-page DSM-II became a 500-page hardbound tome that "vastly expanded the manual's scope, turning it into an entirely new psychopathology of everyday life."

The taxonomy kept growing—from 106 disorders in 1952 to more than 300 in the current edition. Allan Horwitz and Jerome Wakefield, in The Loss of Sadness, demonstrated how this expansion had turned normal grief and sadness into clinical depression by stripping context from the criteria. Frances himself—who would go on to become the most prominent critic of the DSM-5, waging what Greenberg called a "scorched-earth campaign" against his successors—described the accumulation as the "wholesale imperial medicalization of normality."

But the deeper problem was not the expansion. It was the logic underneath it.

The Gap Between Agreement and Truth

What Spitzer achieved was reliability—the extent to which clinicians using the same checklist would arrive at the same diagnosis. Before the DSM-III, two psychiatrists examining the same patient might produce two entirely different diagnoses. The checklist fixed that. It gave the field a common language.

What reliability is not, however, is validity—the extent to which the diagnosis describes an actual disease. A checklist can produce consistent agreement about a label without that label corresponding to anything real in the body. As Greenberg put it, a doctor who diagnosed strep throat entirely on the basis of symptoms—sore throat, fever, swollen glands—without ever running a culture would be practicing bad medicine. A doctor who diagnosed depression entirely on the basis of symptoms was practicing standard psychiatry.

Spitzer's attempt to make psychiatry look more like medicine had, paradoxically, "only highlighted the differences."

This is the gap I lived inside for years. The labels I received were reliable. Any clinician using the DSM's criteria would likely have arrived at the same diagnosis. They were not valid. They did not correspond to what was actually happening in my brain. The agreement was real. The disease it pointed to was not.

Biology Never Read That Book

By the early 2000s, the gap between psychiatry's categories and the biology they claimed to represent had become impossible to ignore from within the field itself.

Thomas Insel, after thirteen years leading the National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH)—the largest funder of mental health research in the world—announced that the agency would reorient its research away from DSM categories entirely. The manual's diagnoses, he said, were still based on nothing more than consensus about symptom clusters. He told The New York Times: "As long as the research community takes the DSM to be a bible, we'll never make progress. Biology never read that book."

That sentence appeared in 2013, more than three decades after the DSM-III had promised to ground psychiatry in science. The promise remained substantially unfulfilled. The field had achieved agreement. It had not achieved understanding.

Source: Ian Panelo/Pexels

What the Lantern Can and Cannot Do

None of this means the DSM should be abandoned. Frances himself—after all the blistering critiques—argued that its categories are "useful constructs," provisional frameworks that capture how people commonly suffer, even if they cannot explain why. For many patients, a diagnosis brings the first coherent name for a lifetime of experiences that had previously resisted language. That matters. Even a rough syntax is better than silence.

But there is a version of a psychiatrist who knows what the DSM is—who treats it as a first approximation, a working hypothesis, an invitation to keep asking—and a version who does not. The version who does not is the one who handed me a label fitted for someone else's suffering and closed the inquiry. The version who knows would have understood that naming is not the same as knowing—that between the description and the disease, there is always a gap, and that patients live inside that gap, sometimes for years, sometimes nearly dying there.

The DSM is a lantern, not a destination. It illuminates a small circle around the clinician's feet. What it cannot reach, it tends to declare does not exist. I know something about living in that darkness. I know what it costs.

The question—for psychiatry, for families, for anyone who has watched a diagnosis land on someone they love and wondered whether it fit—is not whether we need a map. We do. The question is whether we can learn to hold the map more lightly, to remember that the territory is always larger than the map can show, and to keep walking when the lantern's light runs out.
